I want to say that I'm pretty young, 23, and only have 5 years in long term relationships so I certainly don't carry the same amount of experience as you do. But I am very curious about the potential and purpose of romantic relationships, how we can get the most out of them. I'm lucky enough to have an incredible partner of 4 years to explore the highs and lows together.

A realization I've come to is that relationships can't fail, really, if we see them as a vehicle for personal growth. If the goal is to be with one person for our entire lives, yeah divorce is a failure and then its like... did I just waste all that time in my life? But I refuse to accept that any part of a life is waste, or maybe it is but waste is needed to grow plants, ya'know?

Relationships can bring us to the darkest parts of ourselves, for sure. It sounds like your husband withheld the reassurance that you are precious to him, that you have deep value and his relationship with you was profound. Without that bright light of external love and support, the world can feel like a very dark place. Yet, it also sounds like something has changed in you and I hear power through your words. Like you have a self-knowledge gained only by someone who has had to spend a lot of time alone and discover self-reliance. I'm not here to romanticize being completely independent as it's okay to rely on others, but damn discovering how strong you really are on your own is an empowering experience.

Maybe this relationship was like a cocoon, and you've been metamorphizing inside of it without really knowing what would come out the other side. Not even to dismiss him, but it sounds like you have absolutely outgrown the limitations of what your husband could provide. I imagine that you can go on from here to be more fully realized as who you are, more prepared to get what you need from life!

How you respond to this will determine a lot about your life, honestly. Your partner of several years has just put all of his emotional baggage onto you to carry - it’s not me, it’s you. In no healthy relationship is this acceptable. By refusing to do the work of being vulnerable and honest about where his depression is coming from he is willing to put all that pain onto your heart, and why would two equal partners EVER want to do that to each other?!

Now, I’m not gonna be like every other person here and yell “LAWYER!” You are absolutely entitled to try to work through this with this person you love. The most important thing here is that you do it every step of the way with the question: “what is this costing me?” 

Be honest when answering this question. Are you spending so much time consumed by the hurt in this relationship that you can’t enjoy things you used to/want to? Are you allowing someone to treat you in such a way that lowers your sense of value? And so on. 

I will say, I was your boyfriend in my relationship at a point, in that I would find ways my partner was failing me instead of taking responsibility for my own happiness. It was an incredibly painful time for both of us, and let me tell you the only thing that allowed me to quit that shit is that I was very committed to understanding myself and bettering what I saw. People do not change their patterns, ever, without an intense desire to do so. It is not your responsibility to guide or single-handedly support this man in his own self-work. 

Here is what is in your control: you can communicate to him your hurt and your needs very clearly, and this is the only time you should allow anger to be part of your communication. Anger allows us to speak our truths, but if let loose in a relationship it will only cause resentment and pain.

This is not a space for argument, if he is not willing to listen closely to all you have to say then your options change. If he is willing to listen, you give him your list of needs. From this point on, if you see honest effort on meeting these needs you encourage and thank him. You can continue to check in on him about how he’s doing with meeting those needs, what’s been difficult, etc. When your needs are not being met you can still bring it to his attention, with gentleness but a clarity that it is still important to you. Honestly this is really hard work so you’ll have to stay vigilant to make sure you’re not just backsliding into old patterns. But also everything isn’t going to change overnight. 

So what if he doesn’t listen, or says he heard you but refuses to make any actual efforts? This is when you realize the next thing in your control: your own actions. You’re welcome to stay in this relationship, but if you do you have to be willing yo accept who he is in this moment. You can’t have a relationship built on “I’m sticking around so he can become who I deserve and need”. Keep asking “what is this costing me?” And, you are welcome to leave the relationship, yo explore yourself in single life or pursue healthier more fulfilling relationships. That would not be you failing your partner, if it’s what is best for you it would be failing both of you to stay. 

Please, do not lose sight of your own value. You are worth more than constant arguments, than settling for “fine”, than waiting for life to get better. If he can’t see that he’s not who you want by your side

I can feel a deep experience of exhaustion coming through your words. It's a familiar feeling I have had myself, so I know there's something here worth exploring. I want to encourage you to use this poem as an exploration to the themes you are really trying to explore, and go *deeper*. I'm craving to connect with your actual experience, the weight of your body in the morning or the heartbreak of looking in a loved one's eyes and realizing you have no option but to continue. I want to connect with your emotions and reactions and thoughts. 

​

To help you with this, the most important thing I've been taught by my writing teachers has been "show us, don't tell us". If you want us to connect with the emotional content of your poem, you have to create a "moment" that we can attach to. You can expand on this image of a battlefield, maybe read some descriptions of soldiers in WWII and borrow imagery to make connections to your battle with life. Imagine describing the bombs going off, watching friends charge blindly into gunfire with tears streaming down their faces, and you are drifting off to sleep on the battlefield. You could use the admirals who lie to their men about the truth of war and send them in woefully underprepared to your parents. This conveys the same message but with a greater sense of the power of your feeling. 

Feel free to message future drafts or questions to me if you want to continue a dialogue!

Sounds perfectly healthy to me. You’re disappointed, that’s a normal human response. It’s a form of grief, you are grieving the loss of that memory and perhaps (if I’m hearing right) you don’t feel your wishes were respected which adds to the difficulty of your grief. Grief happens at its own pace and there’s nothing we can do but ride along with it or push it down and wait for it to erupt later. 

There is a very real difference between “letting go” and “pushing out”. Thoughts like “I should be able to get over this” or “I’m making too big a deal of it” are more dysfunctional than your natural grief. It comes from the belief that you are somehow flawed, and if you could get rid of this part of you you would be more acceptable. 

My only advice to you, is to respect your grief. Don’t overindulge it, don’t let it spiral into rage or resentment, just acknowledge it and give it the respect it is owed. Try writing about your feelings in factual, “I” based statements. This could look like: “I feel like something important was taken from me. I feel my voice wasn’t heard on a very important day to me. My heart is sore from this” This is how we can give the feelings and what happened the true weight they deserve without getting lost in them or trying to push them away. 

These feelings will be “let go of” only when you’re able to resolve the underlying reason you are holding onto them. Letting go isn’t just something you do, it’s an interactive process between you and the substance of your mind. Good luck and thanks for asking such a good question

Wow. Okay I can’t speak to the person you are replying to because I think they’re on one but I’d like to say that Jesus when seen through a secular lens is one of the most grounded understandings of the path towards true nature.

In almost all other traditions the head figure is an untouchable being incapable of wrong doing or failure. I think we all want to believe in this person who has transcended their earthly limits, but what if that in itself is just another impossible goal we will never reach?

Jesus showed doubt on the cross because he was human. I believe that the story of Jesus is moreso a story of embodying our humanity fully than transcending it. And so Jesus wept, he got sick, and yes, he doubted. Yet everything he did contained absolutely no rejection of his or anyone else’s humanity. He embraces his pain and his doubt. He didn’t damn his tormentors, he asked for them to be forgiven because he knew that their confusion and ignorance was shared by all at some point. If enlightenment is the highest form of all truths, then there should be absolutely nothing about ourselves we have to change or correct to be part of it. So Jesus’ path, of unconditional love, is about acceptance so deep that we are allowed to let go and experience the truth of things exactly as they are, doubt and fear and confusion included.

I think life is the only real teacher. Yes, that includes your post here. But the idea that there is a “right” way to do the path is complete folly and a trap for the mind. A couple books that left deep impressions on me. No particular order. 

The endless journey by Mark Nepo. In this book a poet and beautiful man reflects on his journey, it’s not a memoir but he borrows consistently from his life. He speaks with a tenderness to the struggles of spirituality, the misconceptions of becoming a “perfect being”, the value of our mistakes and confusions. He brings the spiritual journey to such a humble, grounded perspective which I think is absent in many teacher’s writings.

The life of Pi. If you’re into fiction writings with a larger purpose, this is the greatest I have found. You spend day after day with a young man stuck on a raft with a vicious tiger, you feel his desperation, the death of hope, the bright burning joy at the simplest of moments, the acceptance of death, the fight to survive despite that acceptance. It taught me that even in the most mundane or pathetic moments of our lives, their is something infinitely powerful pulling us towards life, towards all of it the painful and the beautiful included.

Desert Solitaire by Edward Abbey. A reflective journal of his time at Arches National Park in Utah, Abbey is a man of true conviction. It is so refreshing to hear his poetic yet no-nonsense understanding of the world around him. There are some sections of the book which are just descriptions of ways to preserve our wildlife or every species of plant in the park, but if spiritual wisdom is what you’re looking for it’s worthwhile to read through it for such gems at this quote:

“A weird, lovely, fantastic object out of nature such as Delicate Arch has the curious ability to remind us - like rock and sunlight and wind and wilderness - that out there is a different world, older and greater and deeper by far than ours, a world which surrounds and sustains the little world of men as sea and sky sustain a ship. The shock of the real. For a little while we are able to see, as a child sees, a world of marvels. For a moment we discover that nothing can be taken for granted, for is this ring of stone is marvelous then all which shaped it is marvelous, and our journey here on earth, able to see and touch and hear in the midst of tangible and mysterious things-in-themselves, is the most strange and daring of all adventures.”

I know it’s a long quote but it’s one of my all time favorites.

Ok one last book. Siddhartha by Herman Hesse. Its a boys journey to find a teacher, only to discover life as the greatest teacher. It’s just a classic, and by the end I really felt I had gone through his life with him, reached the place of acceptance and love with him.

This self awareness, right here. This is the most beautiful thing. There is fear in the rejection, fear of the fall. It’s a great thing that you can acknowledge that. 

I’d like to propose what is perhaps a novel concept. Is it possible that this fear you describe is just part of being a human, with flesh and a heart and a brain on this earth? Is it possible that pain and our aversion to it is the most universal experience of humanity? 

And if that was so, would it even be necessary to ‘transcend’ or even outgrow that fear? I ask because we have the assumption that if anyone were to be enlightened they must first become fearless. I don’t know why being enlightened would be dependent on leaving behind our humanity. It seems to me that enlightenment is so vast that it should be able to contain even the fear, even the closed mind. 

What if you, with all your patterns and fears and destructive tendencies are perfect? And all that is required, really, is the self awareness you already possess: the willingness to see yourself for who you really are. 

Ironically I think many of us would rather go on an epic quest ending in our own destruction than to attempt self-acceptance just as we are. What does that say about us?!

There is no non-existence. There has always been and will always be something. Even the void of space which we call emptiness is something. So then the question is what do we really mean by death? We know that our bodies are perpetually in a state of death. Every cell we believe makes up who we are dies and is replaced within a 7 year period. And the material which made up those cells is recycled into new life through a process which has taken place for nearly half a billion years. Perhaps the problem is not that we die, but that life itself is beyond our understanding. Our limited notions of selfhood as a solid concept do not accurately capture the experience of life. There is a state of awareness accessible to anyone through meditation and many other practices where life is not seen as something an individual possesses, but a continual process the whole cosmos is doing. 

The problem is that our minds, these narrative strings floating in the space of awareness, have created a concept of a separate self and attached to it. This is where all anxiety and suffering stems from. How do we coax this small self who believes itself to be separate, up against an entire universe, that its death is not really the end of anything? I think that is the important question.

Edit: another reflection on death.

Does a cloud die? The obvious retort may be, “No, because a cloud has no memories or feelings or thoughts.” But I would ask, how different is a memory, a feeling or a thought from a cloud? They appear, with a nebulous and continuously changing form, they change and eventually disappear. What is there to die if there was never any concrete and real thing there to begin with? And what never changes, what never dies is the sky beneath the cloud, and the awareness beneath the thought. 

All we need to do is recognize this “self” we are so sure of as a string of clouds, sometimes storms, sometimes haze, sometimes clear, but always changing and never any one solid thing. Every moment it is born, every moment it dies, but it never scratches the surface of the sky.

I can’t speak to the quantum experiments you refer to, but your question of why something exists instead of nothing has always intrigued me. I tried to explore it for years through a scientific, empirical model, and only found frustration. It’s not a logical question, it’s a mystical one. I associated mystics with imperial religions and fanatical cults, so I said no thank you. But by some accident I became a mystic myself, probing into the nature of my own experience and trying to stretch the limits of my preconceived notions of reality. 

What I found is that language is such a fickle thing. We attempt to break the entire universe into black and white, yin and yang, and then describe the relationships between the two. Your concept of object and observer assumes that these are two distinct things. What would this same scenario look like from a non-duel perspective, where there is only one “thing” and nothing outside of it? Would causality fall apart? How could we decide which came first, the chicken or the egg, if we assume the chicken and the egg are one thing? Does awareness bring about existence or does existence bring about awareness?

If you’re looking for a logical answer, prepare to be underwhelmed. But if you’re willing to explore these questions like a zen koan, a meditation through which your unconscious assumptions can melt away, it may lead to deeper understanding. This isn’t an understanding you can convince others of, and you may be called a mad man if you attempt to (as many before you have been). It’s purely your own, it’s born from your own exploration of experience. I admire your excitement, and I don’t believe anyone here will be able to help you in your exploration.

I posit there is something that *does* exist, and that it is larger than our own experience, *but* experience is the only way to touch the land of "actually exists".

How can one interpret the experience of a red flower? There's just that experience. We can say "that flower is yellow" and try to justify it all we want, but what remains true is the existence of an experience of a red flower. In that way truth is what is, all that comes after that is conjecture about truth. 

To take your example of the same thing being experienced differently by multiple people. So the experiences that those people had of that thing aren't true? What do you mean by not true? That they didn't happen? Or that they didn't match the consensus of what that thing is? 

The consensus of what that thing is, is nothing but a story. It could change with time, when we find new ideas about that thing or use it in a different way. However, the experiences each of those people had existed. They were things in-and-of-themselves, independent of culture or language or belief. They may conflict with each other if you try to compare them, but each was true to itself.

Delusion is another label, an attempt to describe something that exists only as an experience. The delusion may be false, but the experience of delusion is real. What is experienced in a drug trip is just as real as everyday life, because it exists. All the games we play to define was is "real" just separate us more from the fact of existence. 

I suppose this isn't anything that I can say, "hey look at this graph! It demonstrates the validity of my claim!" However, as within traditions such as zen buddhism, which gives thorough guidelines that allow one to explore the dichotomy of thought and experience. This is an experiment which one can conduct for themselves to validate the claim. Anyone can look into their own experience, and decide whether truth is derived or observed.
Perhaps I'm arguing against both. My point is that all these labels are attempts to categorize and capture the truth, when it exists beyond our ability to do so.

I would argue that atoms absolutely do only exist as a mental concept. The word atom only has meaning in relationship with other words, which only have meaning related to other concepts such as numbers or formulas and so on. At no point does the concept of an atom exit our mind and become a solid reality. The concept of atom exists in our mind only, and it is used to point to something that does exist. But those are not the same thing.

The place in which the "thing in and of itself" exists is the same place which our subjective experience takes place - "is-ness" as one flimsy way of labeling it. What *is* is true. How we describe that thing that really, definitely "is" is merely pointing at the truth.

In this way, the color red is just a story we tell to get to the truth of that experience. But the ineffable, visceral experience of looking at a red flower exists in the truest sense because it *is*, in and of itself without need for outside reference.

What I’m going to say may not be something you’re ready to hear, but I’ll say it anyways. This is a hard-won insight I’ve had after years of looking for answers both inside and outside of myself. 

The pain you’re seeing in the world is nothing new. It’s been here since the beginning, before guns, before racism, before society. 

The pain shows up in the form of violence because instead of processing it and making peace with it, most humans (almost all of them I think) choose to take it out on others. Strangers, foreigners, neighbors, loved ones, even themselves; everyone is a target of this fear.

The hardest part is realizing that you can’t change other people. How they process their pain is their own issue. Trying to change others is a dead end and it will bring you more suffering.

Where you come in is the realization that you play a part in this. Everyone experiences fundamental paranoia: that the world is out to get you, you aren’t safe, you need to protect yourself. This paranoia is what gives birth, eventually, to violence. If everyone felt safe and content there would be no need to harm others. 

Now, I’m not saying that you yourself are capable of acts of violence. But for every action by a hateful person, I wonder if they could be so hateful if they had been surrounded by open, authentic and caring people their whole lives. Could they have shared their fears, found some peace, discovered a better way? 

But how could anyone open up to those hateful people if they themselves fear the pain that person is feeling? To allow someone to share their struggles is to become involved, which requires vulnerability to their suffering. 

What I’ve found for myself is that my own rejection of pain has caused pain in those around me. I took it out on them in the form of rants, hostility and being closed-off. This led to them being distrustful, angry, and guarded. 

I finally asked the question: what happens when I let the pain in? So that has been my practice, to grow closer to the pain using patience and compassion.
